articles.title: Uzbekistan and Denmark seek to expand investment cooperation - UzDaily.uz
articles.summary: Uzbekistan and Denmark seek to expand investment cooperation  UzDaily.uz
articles.full_text:
Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Uzbekistan and Denmark discussed expanding trade, economic and investment cooperation, with particular attention to water management, equipment localization, energy, agriculture and digital solutions.
The talks were held as part of a business roundtable attended by representatives of government agencies and businesses from both countries. In 2025, trade turnover between Uzbekistan and Denmark increased by 26.6%.
Uzbekistan’s Deputy Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade Akrom Aliyev noted that the current level of investment and trade and economic cooperation between the two countries remains limited.
At the same time, he said the first official visit by Denmark’s foreign minister to Uzbekistan creates additional opportunities for developing bilateral ties.
The Danish delegation visiting Uzbekistan included representatives of leading companies. Around 15 Uzbek private companies participated in the business roundtable.
Water management was one of the key areas of the talks. The sides discussed the introduction of water-saving technologies, the use of new and energy-efficient pumps, and opportunities to localize their production in Uzbekistan at a later stage.
Jens Holst-Nielsen, a representative of the Confederation of Danish Industry, noted Danish businesses’ interest in finding local partners. According to him, companies are also considering cooperation opportunities in agriculture, energy and healthcare.
Particular attention at the meeting was paid to food production and the development of the agro-industrial sector, localization and expanding export potential. The sides also discussed mechanisms for long-term and concessional financing of projects in industry, energy, water management, agriculture, healthcare and logistics.
A memorandum of understanding between Danish company AVK International and an Uzbek water supply partner was signed as a practical outcome of the meeting. The sides intend to implement a joint pilot project.
AVK International Deputy Director for Development Alyona Moiseenko said the company produces equipment for water and gas supply networks, as well as for agriculture and industry.
According to her, the Danish company expects to further expand cooperation and use its products in various regions of Uzbekistan.
Participants in the business roundtable also noted the availability of a legal framework and conditions for foreign investors to operate in Uzbekistan.

articles.title: A 'new front' has emerged in the US-China strategic competition, with a Central Asian nation being named. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: A 'new front' has emerged in the US-China strategic competition, with a Central Asian nation being named.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
According to Argus Media , a provider of energy and commodity information, global tungsten prices have risen by more than 200% since May 2025, adding to the urgency of efforts to develop alternative sources of supply.
 The price escalation comes after Beijing imposed export controls on certain tungsten products in February 2025, amid a market already facing supply shortages from mines and pressure from increased demand from the defense industry.
 Supply shortages have significantly impacted oilfield equipment manufacturers in the US, as the cost of producing drill bits has increased due to material shortages, forcing companies to redesign one of the most crucial tools in oil and gas exploration.
 According to Ulterra Drilling Technologies, the cost of producing drill bits has increased by 50% over the past year. In response, the company is shifting production towards drill bits with steel bodies, although tungsten-rich drill bits generally offer greater durability when drilling through hard, abrasive rock.
 "If tungsten prices are unstable, manufacturers will be forced to switch to steel alternatives," the Commercial Director of Varel Energy Solutions also stated.
 According to data from the U.S. Geological Survey, China currently accounts for nearly 80% of global tungsten production, with output approximately 3.7 times greater than the total output of the rest of the world.
 The dominant position of the world's second-largest economy is not limited to mining but extends to processing and manufacturing. By releasing more of this metal onto the market, Beijing will put rival nations in a difficult position.
 Highly valued for its hardness and heat resistance, tungsten is commonly used in industry to manufacture tools and some military equipment such as armor-piercing rounds and missiles. Additionally, this metal is used in the semiconductor and electronic component industries for artificial intelligence (AI) hardware and data centers.
 Despite being a major consumer of tungsten, the United States has ceased commercial tungsten mining operations since 2015. This dependence has made overseas projects increasingly important to Washington's efforts to secure a supply of the metal. 
|  | 
| The race to break China 's monopoly on tungsten supply is shifting to Kazakhstan, where US-backed mining projects are vying for competition. (Source: SCMP) | 
 A new front for the two superpowers.
 In April, the US mining investment company Cove Capital acquired a 70% stake in two mineral mines in Kazakhstan's Karaganda region: Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty. The total estimated development cost for the two projects is $1.1 billion. Both projects are currently in the engineering design and feasibility study phases, with the goal of beginning production in 2028.
 This timeline differs from other investments China is pouring into the Central Asian nation. Jiaxin International Resources currently operates the Boguty mine in the Almaty region of Kazakhstan. The mine began trial production in November 2024 and is scheduled to commence commercial operations in April 2025.
 Another tungsten mining investment project – involving Kunxin International Investment and Kazakhstan's SP Saryarka Tungsten – was also among the more than 60 agreements signed at the Belt and Road Summit in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region in September 2026, although very few details about this project have been released.
 Professor Liang Yan, an economics professor at Willamette University (USA), argues that this difference in development pace has given China an immediate advantage in the supply chain. According to her, China has already begun production, while US-backed projects still need to complete research, secure funding, and build infrastructure.
 With reserves exceeding two million tons, Kazakhstan is projected to become a "key tungsten producer," potentially supplying approximately 15% of global annual production. "I don't think US funding can offset China's leading advantage in processing capacity and trade scale," said expert Liang Yan. 
|  | 
| Kazakhstan is projected to become a "key tungsten producer," with the potential to supply approximately 15% of global annual production. (Source: Times of Central Asia) | 
 The challenge for the US doesn't stop at bringing new mines into operation. According to Liang Yan, Kazakhstan also needs to develop more on-site refining capacity if it wants to build a supply chain less dependent on China. Without this capacity, new mines may still have to send concentrates to Beijing's processing facilities in case alternative facilities experience delays or increased costs.
 Liu Wenjing, a member of the mining sector executive board at the Astana International Finance Centre and founder and chief advisor of Elistra Advisory, acknowledged that funding from the US could significantly reduce barriers to building an alternative tungsten supply chain.
 "Capital cannot automatically replicate the industrial system that China has painstakingly built over the past decades," she said.
 This expert argues that China's advantages extend across almost all stages of the tungsten supply chain. These advantages range from processing raw ore into concentrates, producing ammonium paratungsten (APT) – a crucial intermediate in the manufacture of tungsten products – to producing finished products such as cemented carbides.
 Geographical factors also play a significant role. Kazakhstan borders China, while shipments to Europe and North America must follow longer routes, including crossings of the Caspian Sea. Liu, a former board secretary at Jiaxin, commented: “The U.S. has effectively realized that simply investing in overseas mines is not enough to solve the problem.”
 This strategy is clearly demonstrated by Washington's investment in domestic processing capacity, including plans to convert tungsten into APTs. In mid-September, Washington announced a $450 million investment in Elmet Corporation through the purchase of redeemable preferred stock.
 "This shows that the US strategy is shifting from simply securing ore supplies to filling the gap in intermediate processing," Liu analyzed.
 A similar mindset applies to transportation. Specifically, the Northern Katpar project is being designed to access international markets via the Trans-Caspian route. According to Mr. Liu, these plans show that Western-backed projects are focusing on getting the metal to buyers, not just on extraction.
 The price of dependence
 Efforts to develop alternative supply routes have intensified since China implemented export licensing regulations in February 2025 – the same time that new US tariffs on Chinese goods began to take effect.
 At the same time, China has only granted export licenses to 15 tungsten companies under its state-managed trade system for the period of 2026 and 2027. Products subject to control from 2025 onwards will still have to comply with separate regulations regarding export licenses and end-user inspection procedures.
 Although Beijing has claimed that these control measures are aimed at protecting national security and fulfilling its non-proliferation obligations, public opinion views these efforts as part of the trade and technological competition between the world's two leading superpowers.
 Chinese customs data shows that exports of tungsten products (by weight) decreased by 25% year-on-year in the first eight months of 2026. Exports of sodium tungstate fell sharply by 94.9%, while exports of ammonium paratungstate – a key intermediate material – decreased by 89.3%.
 Exports of tungsten-related products from China to the US also decreased by 21% in volume compared to the same period last year. Exports of unprocessed tungsten and tungsten carbide have ceased entirely, while exports of tungsten bars decreased by 42%.
 Restrictions, coupled with scarce supply from mines and increased demand, have added further pressure to push prices higher.
 Rising costs are also prompting Washington to seek additional sources of supply besides mining at new mines, including recycling. On August 27, the U.S. imposed a one-year ban on tungsten scrap exports to retain this resource for domestic processing businesses.
 According to the materials research platform Material Insights, recycled tungsten accounts for approximately 25 to 30% of the global supply and is particularly important to the United States due to its lack of domestic mining operations.
 The race is spreading globally.
 For Kazakhstan, the key issue is the speed of implementation of the proposed mining and processing projects. Currently, Kazakhstan contributes less than 3% of global tungsten production, although new projects could significantly increase the Central Asian nation's market share.
 According to estimates by EarthRarest – a research and investment platform focusing on strategic metals – Kazakhstan's 2.8% share of global mining output is equivalent to about one-eighth of total production outside of China.
 "Having an additional reliable supply source is significant for buyers looking to diversify their sourcing, although this will not change China's leading position," EarthRarest predicts.
 EarthRarest says that Kazakhstan's tungsten has the potential to reach Western buyers without going through China, provided that the mining, processing, transportation, and customer agreements are all feasible. 
|  | 
| A tungsten mining site in Inner Mongolia, China, in October 2025. (Source: Xinhua News Agency) | 
 Kazakhstan is not alone; many countries are also striving to secure their tungsten supply and increase the value derived from this mineral resource.
 In late August 2026, the UK's National Wealth Fund announced an investment of £71 million in Tungsten West to support plans to restart the Hemerdon tungsten and tin mine in Devon. The project aims to reach full production capacity by the first quarter of 2027.

articles.title: Afghanistan Dispute and Russia’s Ties With India Limit Moscow-Islamabad Cooperation - خبرگزاری اطلس
articles.summary: Afghanistan Dispute and Russia’s Ties With India Limit Moscow-Islamabad Cooperation  خبرگزاری اطلس
articles.full_text:
The Pakistani newspaper Dawn, in an analysis, has written that conflicting Russian and Pakistani interests over Afghanistan, along with Moscow’s longstanding ties with India, are preventing the formation of broad cooperation between Russia and Islamabad. Mohammad Amir Rana, a security analyst and head of the Pakistan Institute for Peace Studies, says Russia’s caution stems more from the two countries’ differing regional views than from their tense past.
According to the analysis, the sharp differences in the two countries’ economic and defence relations also limit Pakistan’s standing with Russia. The volume of bilateral trade between Pakistan and Russia is estimated at less than $500 million, while trade between Russia and India stands at about $69 billion. Rana also wrote that Moscow’s defence cooperation with Islamabad is selective and falls well short of the level of military cooperation Russia has with India, including joint research and production and after-sales services.
Dawn wrote that despite India’s diversification of its defence partners, there is no clear sign of a fundamental deterioration in Moscow-New Delhi relations. According to Rana, Russia’s interest in Pakistan is more geopolitical in nature, and maintaining ties with Islamabad keeps Moscow’s channels open with Pakistani political and security leaders, including figures close to Donald Trump, the president of the United States.
The analysis also says differences over Afghanistan are among the factors limiting cooperation: Russia has recognised the Taliban administration, but Pakistan sees Afghanistan as a source of terrorist threats inside the country. Rana says Russia wants Afghanistan linked with its Central Asian allies, while Pakistan shares interests with the United States on parts of this issue; a situation that, he says, also does not align with China’s desire to keep the US away from the region. The analysis concludes that the shared interests of Russia and Pakistan are limited when it comes to building a broad strategic partnership.

articles.title: India's Role in Ending Russia-Ukraine Conflict Grows: Ukraine Official - indianewsnetwork.com
articles.summary: India's Role in Ending Russia-Ukraine Conflict Grows: Ukraine Official  indianewsnetwork.com
articles.full_text:
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has stated that India's proposal to help resolve the ongoing conflict with Russia is the most extensive and broad yet presented. He made these comments on Friday, highlighting India's willingness to take an active role in mediating the situation, as reported by RBC-Ukraine.
Sybiha noted that this marked the first time India had indicated an intent to play such a mediatory role in the conflict that erupted following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which has led to significant loss of life and widespread destruction. He mentioned that Ukraine has received proposals from other nations as well, including Egypt, Turkey, and the United States.
The Foreign Minister elaborated on potential avenues for peace, stating that Ukraine is open to considering an energy and agricultural truce in the Black Sea. This truce would necessitate a complete halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, especially in port areas, which have seen escalating violence and damage, including incidents involving shipping vessels and civilians.
Sybiha also revealed that Kyiv is investigating the possibility of an unconditional ceasefire along the frontline with Russia, which could pave the way for future negotiations. Russian President Vladimir Putin acknowledged Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s contributions to proposing viable solutions, describing them as “very good ideas.”
However, Putin dismissed an immediate cessation of long-range strikes, insisting that intensified military actions had to continue. He pointedly rejected suggestions that attacks on energy facilities could end if Russian attacks on Ukrainian ships were curtailed, labelling such conditionality as ridiculous.
The evolving dialogue suggests that while progress may hinge on broader international mediation, the situation remains complex and fluid. Analysts will be closely watching how India's involvement could shape the future course of the conflict and international relations in the region.

articles.title: US to receive potash shipment from Belarus as relations thaw - Financial Times
articles.summary: US to receive potash shipment from Belarus as relations thaw  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Your guide to what Trump’s second term means for Washington, business and the world
The first US-bound shipment of Belarusian potash in four years is expected to arrive at a New Orleans port within weeks as Washington pursues a diplomatic opening with Minsk.
The Belarusian Potash Company loaded 30,000 tonnes of granular muriate of potash (MOP) on to a Marshall Islands-owned ship at Russia’s Bronka port in St Petersburg on September 15, according to pricing agency Argus.
It is expected to offload at a port in New Orleans, Louisiana, on October 14, according to ship-tracking data from commodities platform Kpler.
The shipment is the first to be sent to the US since Washington began to ease sanctions on the Belarusian potash industry in December last year as part of a wider deal to secure the release of political prisoners.
The US imposed sanctions on the country’s potash industry, one of its principal exports, in 2021 after President Alexander Lukashenko violently cracked down on pro-democracy protests the previous year.
Between 2017 and 2021, an average of 635,000 tonnes of potash were exported from Belarus to the US, according to Argus.
Potash is commonly used as a fertiliser that adds potassium to the soil and boosts crop yields.
Global availability of fertiliser has become increasingly short as a result of the Middle East conflict, which has all but closed the Strait of Hormuz.
While an increasing number of oil tankers have been shuttling through the waterway, incentivised by record-breaking freight rates, margins on other commodities are not enough to offset the potential risk of being hit by Iran.
Gulf countries are major producers of nitrogen-based fertiliser as well as urea and phosphates.
In September, Donald Trump said that the US was working on a “massive deal” to buy the fertiliser from Belarus in a post on social media.
Trump claimed that the imports would cost “substantially less” than the US is paying to Canada, which is locked in a stand-off with Washington over trade. Canada accounts for almost 80 per cent of US potash imports.
“This shipment serves a few purposes: it acts as a political gesture amid trade tensions between the US and Canada,” said Katsiaryna Shmatsina, Eurasia fellow with the Lawfare Institute. “On the Belarusian side, Minsk is heavily motivated to seize this opening with a major global power.”
Analysts remain sceptical that Belarus can rapidly scale up its exports to the US in the near future or compete with Canadian prices.
“The main rationale behind Trump’s big potash deal is calming down the base ahead of the midterms as well as calming down the Belarusians,” said Balázs Jarábik, partner at the analysis firm R Politik, noting that Minsk has been frustrated that Belarusian businesses were struggling to re-enter the global market after the US lifted sanctions.
EU sanctions prohibit Belarus from using Lithuania’s Klaipėda port, the fastest route to sea, forcing shipments to take a more expensive and circuitous route from Russia.
Lukashenko has also noted that all of Belarus’s potash has been contracted for 2026.
The shipment of Belarusian potash represents a fraction of the 5.6mn tonnes of potash imported by the US last year. But it is the latest sign of a cautious thaw in ties between the US and Belarus, which has been internationally isolated over its violent suppression of dissent and role in enabling Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Trump’s special envoy for Belarus John Coale has made multiple trips to the country, securing the release of hundreds of political prisoners in exchange for sanctions relief.
Coale was recently nominated to serve as Trump’s special presidential envoy for hostage affairs. In an interview with the FT, he said that he was in early talks about brokering a deal between Russia and Ukraine on the release of civilian prisoners.
Lukashenko has long played Russia and the west off against each other, but analysts have noted that the prospects of drawing Minsk out of Moscow’s orbit are low.

articles.title: Between Washington and Beijing: Can Central Asia Preserve Its Multi-Vector Technology Policy? - atalayar.com
articles.summary: Between Washington and Beijing: Can Central Asia Preserve Its Multi-Vector Technology Policy?  atalayar.com
articles.full_text:
According to a draft letter from the U.S. State Department seen by Reuters, the issue concerns 35 countries that signed the American AI Opportunity Statement adopted in June. The draft letter warns that these countries may not be able to participate simultaneously in the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative and a competing Chinese initiative on artificial intelligence.
As AI becomes increasingly connected to semiconductor manufacturing, critical minerals, energy, data centers, computing capacity and national security, Central Asian countries will face growing pressure over their choice of technology partners.
Is it realistic to expect Central Asian countries to choose between American and Chinese AI ecosystems?
It is realistic to expect Washington to become increasingly demanding about where its partners stand on certain sensitive technologies. It is much less realistic, however, to expect Central Asian countries to abandon their multi-vector foreign policies and choose one technology ecosystem at the expense of the other.
This distinction is fundamental. The United States increasingly views artificial intelligence not simply as an economic sector, but as a strategic technology ecosystem that includes advanced semiconductors, computing capacity, data centers, critical minerals, energy infrastructure, research networks, technology standards and investment.
From Washington’s perspective, a country’s participation in China-linked initiatives such as WAICOmay therefore raise questions that go far beyond AI regulation itself. The American argument is that technology partnerships can create long-term dependencies and may potentially facilitate the transfer, spread or circumvention of restrictions on technologies that Washington considers strategically sensitive.
This is why the State Department draft letter is important, even though, according to available information, it has not yet been sent to its recipients and its contents may still change. The main message behind the initiative appears to be that Washington sees participation in Pax Silica not simply as membership in another international forum, but as a strategic commitment.
WAICO and Pax Silica are not mirror-image organizations: One important point should be kept in mind: WAICO and Pax Silica should not be treated as fully symmetrical organizations. Pax Silica is primarily focused on the security and resilience of critical technology supply chains — from minerals and energy to semiconductors, computing infrastructure and artificial intelligence.
Based on available information, WAICO places much greater emphasis on building national capacity, international AI governance, access to technology, workforce development and greater participation by developing countries in the emerging global AI ecosystem.
It may therefore be more accurate to describe them not as two identical “AI blocs”, but as two competing approaches to the emerging technological order. The American approach can be broadly described as: “Secure the technology ecosystem. ” The Chinese approach is more focused on another idea: “Expand access to the technology ecosystem. ”
For countries in the Global South, the second approach is particularly attractive. This does not mean that China is acting purely out of altruism. By providing infrastructure, equipment, AI models, training and technology platforms, Beijing gains clear strategic advantages. The wider use of Chinese technologies also helps spread Chinese standards, products and institutional practices.
Independent research on WAICO highlights precisely this dual nature. On the one hand, the organization may strengthen China’s international influence. On the other, it responds to a genuine demand from developing countries for training, infrastructure, access to open-weight models and a greater role in shaping international AI rules.
At the same time, the AI race is entering a new phase. China is no longer simply catching up with the United States. It is competing with the U.S. in performance, cost and scale of deployment. According to Stanford HAI, in March 2026 the gap between the leading American and Chinese AI models was only 2.7%. Since the beginning of 2025, models from the two countries have repeatedly exchanged the lead.
China is strengthening its position through DeepSeek, Kimi K3, Qwen, GLM and MiniMax — open-weight models, rapid development and significantly lower operating costs. Price may become one of the most important factors in the next stage of the AI race. The US still has major advantages: advanced chips and computing infrastructure, capital and leading AI research laboratories. In 2025, U.S. developers produced 59 notable AI models, compared with 35 in China.
But China’s strategy is different: Open models + low cost + industrial scale + government support + rapid deployment. The key question is therefore no longer simply who has the most powerful AI. It is increasingly about who can make advanced AI cheap, accessible and widely available.
That could determine not only technological leadership, but also geopolitical influence in the global AI race. For Central Asia, this distinction is particularly important. Central Asia: Diversification, Not Choosing Sides. The foreign policy model of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and other Central Asian countries has traditionally been based on diversification rather than exclusive alignment with a single external partner.
Their goal is not so much to balance ideologically between the United States and China as to avoid excessive dependence on any one external power while attracting investment, technology, infrastructure and access to different markets.
This approach is particularly rational in the technology sector. Central Asian countries do not have sufficient resources to build a complete modern AI ecosystem entirely on their own.
Building competitive AI infrastructure requires not only skilled professionals, but also substantial financial investment, access to advanced technologies and integration into global technology chains. For most Central Asian countries, building such an ecosystem independently would be extremely expensive and technologically difficult.
The region therefore depends on foreign capital, advanced GPUs and computing capacity, cloud platforms, telecommunications equipment and investment in data centers. International research partnerships, training for engineers and tech-specialists, and access to global markets and tech-platformsare equally important.
In other words, the key question for Central Asia is not whether the region can build its own AI ecosystem completely from scratch. The real question is whether it can integrate effectively into the global AI infrastructure while attracting the technology, capital and expertise it needs. That is why international technology and investment cooperation is not simply an additional advantage. It is a necessary condition for building a competitive AI economy in Central Asia.
The economic cost of cutting cooperation with one of the world’s two largest technology centers could therefore be very high. At the same time, Central Asia possesses resources that both sides need. The region has strategic importance because of its energy resources, critical minerals, geographic position, growing digital infrastructure and emerging markets.
This gives Central Asian countries some room for maneuver. They should not be seen simply as passive recipients of American or Chinese technologies. Competition among external partners can be used to negotiate better investment terms, local production and technology transfer.
For example, Kazakhstan’s simultaneous engagement with American and Chinese technology and investment partners shows that Astana views technology diversification as part of its national strategy. The same logic applies to a large extent to Uzbekistan, although its economic structure and external partnerships have their own specific features.
For this reason, I would not say that Central Asian countries are already facing an immediate need to “choose sides”. Rather, we are entering a period in which the cost of maintaining genuine technological multi-vectorism will increase.
Where Will Multi-Vectorism Face Limits?
The main problem is that U.S.-China competition is gradually creating two technology ecosystems that may become incompatible in the most sensitive areas. A country can use Chinese technologies in commercial and civilian applications while cooperating with the United States on initiatives aimed at strengthening the resilience of global supply chains.
However, the room for such technological balancing becomes much smaller when it comes to advanced GPUs, dual-use technologies, military AI applications, sensitive government data, high-performance computing and advanced semiconductor manufacturing. Infrastructure directly affected by U.S. export controls is particularly important. In these areas, Washington is likely to demand greater transparency and increasingly seek restrictions on the use of certain Chinese technologies and suppliers.
At the same time, Beijing may be less comfortable with a situation in which a country actively uses Chinese technology infrastructure while participating in initiatives designed to reduce China’s role in strategic technology supply chains. This creates a new strategic dilemma for countries that want to cooperate with both the United States and China. Technological neutrality is becoming increasingly difficult precisely where AI, semiconductors, data and computing capacity intersect with national security.
As a result, choosing a technology partner may gradually stop being purely an economic decision and become a question of foreign policy and strategic positioning.
